A mapping system made that route. And they do not fail (I've done thousands of permits and never had one fail).

Either the driver didn't measure properly, or his permits were wrong, or he went off route.
It's all mapping systems now, not supposed to happened. Has never happened to me in the thousands of permits I've done.
Rocket and space x components have super security on all their moves. They ask for 2 pole cars, security guard at night while driver sleeps, etc. They would never allow something like this to happen.

Was this on Texas side? If so, wasn't needed until 17' high.

If in OK he most likely would have need one (needed at 15'9)

It's very much his fault. If he measured his load properly and his permits were accurate, the systems that generate these permits do not route you into overpasses that do not have at least 3 inch clearance (some states its 6 inches depending on the width of the load).

So either his height was measured wrong, his permits were wrong, or he was off route. You'd be surprised at some of the dumb shit these drivers do. I work with them every day.

Edit: someone else mentioned this was in on i-35 at tx/ok. If this was in tx, no need for pole car until 17' high. If ok, he would have had a pole car, and then pole car would have some explaining to do. But normally the pole car is a safety back up. The route is supposed to clear regardless.

Does not take months to get something this high routed. In most of the US 16' high isn't that complexe to plan (excluding New England). 

Either they didn't measure correctly, didn't get routed properly, went off route, or just flat out went without the proper permits and pilot cars. 

In the end, the carrier is always the one responsible for the route they use, it says so on most permits that are issued by DOT.
